learning.analogy: Learning is like climbing stairs. You can only reach the third step if the first two are solid.
learning.reason: If you try to memorize a whole framework before you ever run one small example, most of it slips away. Learning in small loops (read, guess, try, check, review) shows you exactly which step you missed.

terms.prerequisite: something you need to know first, before the next thing makes sense
terms.checkpoint: a question you answer from memory, without peeking
terms.contract: a clear promise about what goes in and what comes out

facts: Read the prerequisites before you run a framework example.
Guess the output first, then look at the answer.
When a test fails, it points to the idea you are missing.
A practice score in this app is just a helper, not an official exam grade.
Come back to a topic after a break; remembering it is better practice than just re-reading it.
learning.scenario: You understand how to ask for data with GET, but you cannot explain how the server checks incoming data. What should you study next?
choices: Practice sending bad data and see how the server checks it
Jump straight to advanced deployment
Copy an answer without trying it
Switch frameworks so the problem goes away

history.analogy: A new tool is like a bicycle. It gets you there faster than walking, but now you have a bike to look after.
history.reason: Programmers got tired of repeating the same boring setup, so languages and frameworks were invented to do it for them. Each one saves time but brings something new to learn and maintain. Pick the smallest tool that really solves your problem.

terms.runtime: the helper program that actually runs your code
terms.framework: a ready-made skeleton that calls your code at the right moments
terms.tradeoff: a good thing you get in exchange for a cost you accept

facts: A runtime runs your program; a package manager downloads the libraries it needs.
A framework saves setup work, but it does not decide who is allowed to do what.
Code that is compiled once to portable bytecode still needs a matching runtime on each computer.
Non-blocking input and output helps when your program mostly waits; it does not make heavy math faster.
When you pick a technology, say which need it meets and which cost you accept.
history.scenario: A small team spends most of its time writing the same route and checking code over and over. What is a good reason to add a framework?
choices: It removes repeated setup while the team still writes its own permission rules
It guarantees every database query is fast
It means you no longer need tests
It automatically decides who is allowed to do what

types.analogy: A type is the label on a box. Validation is opening the box to check that what is inside really matches the label.
types.reason: Data from outside your program can have any shape, and a wrong shape can cause strange problems far away from where it entered. Types help you reason about your own code, but you still have to check data when it arrives from the outside.

terms.type: a description of what kind of values are allowed
terms.reference: a pointer to an object, not the object itself
terms.validation: checking real data against a rule

facts: A type annotation does not check the JSON that actually arrives.
Check unknown input before you use it.
Equal values have the same content; the same object is the very same thing in memory.
Missing, null, blank, and zero can all mean different things.
Refuse bad input before you save it.
types.scenario: Someone sends a note title that is only spaces. What should the API do?
choices: Trim it, see it is empty, and reject it
Trust the type label and accept it
Save the spaces as a real title
Crash and show a scary error

functions.analogy: A function is a little machine: you drop things in the input tray, it works, and something comes out of the output tray.
functions.reason: If you copy the same steps in many places, the copies slowly become different and cause bugs. A function holds one rule in one place so everything uses it the same way and you can test it alone.

terms.parameter: a named slot where a function receives an input
terms.return: the answer a function hands back
terms.scope: the part of the program where a name can be seen

facts: A function's parameters are part of its promise to callers.
A pure function only works with what you give it and changes nothing outside.
Do not hide a shared changeable list inside a default value.
Returning a value lets the caller decide what to do with it.
A small function can be tested without starting a whole web server.
functions.scenario: Three routes all clean up a note title in slightly different ways. What fixes this?
choices: Move the cleanup into one tested function that all three use
Copy all the routes again
Only check the title in the user interface
Return success even when there is no title

collections.analogy: Collections are shelves. A list keeps things in order, a set never allows two of the same, and a map lets you find a thing by its label.
collections.reason: Searching a long list one item at a time gets slow as it grows. If you pick the right container for how you will look things up, the code is clearer and faster.

terms.list: items in order; the same item can appear twice
terms.set: a bag of items where each one appears only once
terms.map: a lookup table that connects each key to one value

facts: A list keeps the order and allows repeats.
A set is how you say 'no duplicates'.
A map connects each key to exactly one current value.
Sorting needs a clear rule for what 'smaller' means.
A database index helps find things in big stored data; a map in memory disappears when the program stops.
collections.scenario: You often need to find a note by its unique ID in a small program. Which container fits best?
choices: A map where the note ID is the key
A list you search from the start every time
A set that stores no notes
One big changeable text string

objects.analogy: A class is a blueprint. An object is one real house built from it, with its own paint color and furniture.
objects.reason: If anyone can change any field at any time, rules get broken. Putting data and the actions that use it together, and guarding the data, keeps every object valid.

terms.class: a blueprint that describes the data and actions of something
terms.object: one real thing built from a class
terms.invariant: a rule that must always be true for the object

facts: A constructor should create an object that is already valid.
Private data is changed only through carefully written methods.
Composition means one object uses another object to help it.
A child class should keep the promises of its parent class.
A record is a simple value holder, but things inside it can still be changeable.
objects.scenario: A note must never have an empty title. Where should the object protect that rule?
choices: When it is created and whenever the title changes
Only in a color on the screen
Only in a comment in the database
Only in a log message

interfaces.analogy: An interface is the shape of a wall socket. Any plug that fits the shape works, no matter which brand made it.
interfaces.reason: If your business rules talk straight to one specific database, they are hard to test and hard to change. A small contract says what is needed, and different helpers can fill that role.

terms.interface: a list of actions that something promises to offer
terms.adapter: a piece that connects the promise to a real tool
terms.substitutability: swapping one piece for another without breaking the promise

facts: The service should rely on the repository's promise, not on a specific database.
A fake in-memory version is handy for fast, safe tests.
A real database version must behave the same way as the fake one.
A test double stands in for the outside world, not for the rule you are testing.
An interface cannot fix pieces that behave differently from the promise.
interfaces.scenario: You want to test your service while the PostgreSQL database is switched off. What helps?
choices: Give the service an in-memory stand-in for its repository
Catch every error and pretend the catalog is empty
Put the database password inside the test
Delete the service rules

null.analogy: An empty seat and a seat with a sign saying 'empty' are not the same thing. One is absence, the other is a value.
null.reason: Missing values are normal when data comes from outside. Showing clearly when something is missing prevents surprise crashes and keeps 'not sent' separate from 'sent but wrong'.

terms.null: a marker meaning 'there is no value here'
terms.optional: a box that may hold a value or may be empty
terms.normalization: turning different ways of writing the same thing into one standard form

facts: Clean up text first, then check whether it is blank.
Zero is a real number and does not mean 'missing'.
Look inside an optional box before you take something out.
A bad title and an unknown note ID are different problems.
Do not hide real bugs by pretending they are just missing data.
null.scenario: An update request leaves out the title. With PATCH rules, what should happen to the title?
choices: Keep the current title unless the contract says otherwise
Replace it with an empty string
Delete the whole note
Treat the missing title as permission to do anything

errors.analogy: Errors are road signs. They tell the driver what happened without showing the inside of the engine.
errors.reason: Raw crashes leak private details and confuse people. Turn known problems into clear, steady messages, and keep the private details in logs that only your team sees.

terms.exception: a problem that interrupts the normal flow of a program
terms.safeError: a short message that is safe to show to the person who asked
terms.cause: the deeper problem that explains a surface problem

facts: An unknown ID should give a clear 'not found' answer.
A validation problem must never turn into a fake success.
Whoever opens a resource must close it, even when something fails.
Error messages for callers must not reveal SQL, file paths, secrets, or stack traces.
For surprises, send a general message and a request ID that your team can look up.
errors.scenario: A database error includes a private file path. What should the API send back?
choices: A general safe error with a steady code and a request ID
The raw error text exactly as it came
An empty success answer
The private path, to help debugging

time.analogy: A calendar date and a moment on the clock are different tools, like a wall calendar and a stopwatch.
time.reason: A time without context is confusing because of time zones and daylight saving changes. Store the kind of time you really mean and make every conversion clear.

terms.instant: one exact moment on the world's timeline
terms.localDate: a calendar day with no time zone attached
terms.encoding: the rule for turning text into bytes and back

facts: A store's schedule day is usually a calendar date.
A record of when something happened is usually an instant.
Changing time zones needs a named zone.
The number of characters you see can differ from the length of the string.
Always say which encoding a text file uses.
time.scenario: A shop schedule is about a whole trading day, not one exact moment. What should you store?
choices: A calendar date plus the store's time zone rule
A server time with no explanation
A decimal number of months
A password string

modules.analogy: Modules are labeled drawers. Each drawer holds one kind of tool, so you can find things without digging through a pile.
modules.reason: Putting everything in one huge file hides how pieces depend on each other. Clear drawers help reuse, but too many tiny drawers make it hard to find anything.

terms.module: one piece of code with clear things it takes in and gives out
terms.package: a bundle of modules with a version number
terms.lockfile: a file that records the exact versions you installed

facts: Share only the parts that are meant to be used from outside.
A lockfile makes installs repeatable.
Pieces that depend on each other in a circle are hard to understand.
Different module systems find files in different ways.
Keep secrets out of files you commit.
modules.scenario: Two computers install different versions of the same libraries. What makes builds the same?
choices: A lockfile saved with the project and used by the package manager
A screenshot of the editor
A hidden browser setting
A tag called 'latest' on its own

config.analogy: Configuration is the address label on a parcel. You change where it goes without changing what is inside.
config.reason: If addresses and passwords are typed into the code, you must edit the code for every place it runs. Settings kept outside the code, and checked at startup, let the same program run anywhere.

terms.environment: the settings given to a program by the place it runs
terms.profile: a named set of settings, such as dev or production
terms.secret: a password or key that must never be made public

facts: Check that required settings exist when the program starts.
Keep secrets on the server, never in browser code.
A profile can switch which helper is used without changing the service's promise.
Write down which setting wins when two places disagree.
A missing database password is a problem to report, not an empty catalog.
config.scenario: In production, the storage password is missing. What should the app do when it starts?
choices: Say it is not ready and show a safe configuration error
Start with a fake full library
Put a private key into browser JavaScript
Quietly pretend the storage is empty

http.analogy: An HTTP request is a letter. It has an address, a word saying what you want done, and sometimes a form inside.
http.reason: If every app invented its own message style, nothing could talk to anything else. Shared methods, headers, and status codes let different programs understand each other.

terms.method: the action word of a request, like GET or POST
terms.header: extra information that travels with a message
terms.status: a number in the reply that says how it went

facts: GET reads data and should not create anything new.
Creating something with POST usually answers 201 and points to the new item.
Content-Type tells what kind of data is in the body.
Before retrying a write, decide how to avoid doing it twice.
A list answer should be a limited page in a steady order.
http.scenario: A client wants a page of notes and must not change anything. Which request fits?
choices: GET /notes?limit=20 returning a limited list
POST /delete-everything
A GET that secretly changes data
A database password inside the URL

routing.analogy: A route is a labeled service window. Middleware is the line of checks you pass before you reach the window.
routing.reason: Without a routing table, every handler would have to read every URL. Steps that run before the handler, like size limits and login checks, keep rules in one place, but each handler must still check who may touch which record.

terms.route: a rule that sends a method and a path to a piece of code
terms.binding: turning parts of a request into inputs for your code
terms.middleware: a step that runs around every request

facts: Set the body size limit before code that reads the body.
Knowing who someone is does not replace checking what they may touch.
Path parameters and query parameters play different roles.
A route handles the web side and passes business rules to a service.
An unknown route should give a predictable 'not found' answer.
routing.scenario: A request body is bigger than the allowed upload size. What happens first?
choices: Stop it at the size limit before reading it all
Load every byte into memory, then decide
Send it to every database table
Trust a hidden button in the page

validation.analogy: Validation is the librarian checking your form before going to look at the shelves.
validation.reason: Type labels are not permission checks. Keep the shape check, the clean-up, the business rules, and the ownership check separate so you always know which one failed.

terms.schema: a written description of the shape and limits of data
terms.businessRule: a rule about what is allowed in your app
terms.authorization: deciding what a person is allowed to do

facts: A schema can reject a title that is too long.
Trimming can turn spaces into an empty title that must be rejected.
The service checks that the category is one it allows.
A real note ID does not prove the caller owns that note.
Check the data you send back as well as the data you receive.
validation.scenario: A note ID is real but belongs to someone else. Which check blocks the read?
choices: Checking that the caller owns that record
Only checking the JSON is well-formed
Only checking the secure connection worked
The color of the submit button

database.analogy: A transaction is a sealed envelope handed in at school. Either all the papers are accepted, or none of them are.
database.reason: Plain files and lists do not protect your data when many things happen at once. A database gives you queries and rules, but you still decide where the sealed envelope starts and ends.

terms.transaction: a group of changes that all succeed or all get undone
terms.index: a quick-lookup list a database keeps beside your data
terms.parameter: a value sent separately from the SQL text

facts: Use parameters instead of gluing user text into SQL.
A database rule keeps data safe even when many writes happen at once.
An index speeds some reads but costs space and slows writes a little.
Give a borrowed connection back when the request ends.
Keep big files outside the database rows and store only a pointer.
database.scenario: A note and its bookmark must be created together. How should storage behave?
choices: One transaction that undoes both if either fails
Two separate writes with no recovery plan
Send the database password to the browser
A giant global list that only pretends to save

transactions.analogy: A numbered receipt makes sure the same payment is not charged twice, even if you show it twice.
transactions.reason: A reply can get lost even though the work succeeded. Unique request keys and database rules stop repeats from doing the job twice, and an outbox saves a 'to do later' note in the same step as the work.

terms.idempotency: doing the same action again has no extra effect
terms.outbox: a to-do note saved in the same step as the main change
terms.isolation: how separate changes at the same time are kept from tangling

facts: A timeout does not prove the write failed.
An idempotency key needs a place that stores each key only once.
The outbox note is saved in the same commit as the real data.
Retry only actions where doing them twice is safe.
A version check can spot two people changing the same thing.
transactions.scenario: A create request times out, and the client tries again. How do you avoid a duplicate?
choices: Use the same unique request key and store it only once
Make a new key for every retry
Assume a timeout always means nothing happened
Turn off all error messages

security.analogy: A badge shows who you are. A room key decides which rooms you can enter. They are not the same thing.
security.reason: Trusting a button in the browser, or a suggestion from an AI model, hands your power to the wrong place. Check who the caller is, and check what they may do, on the server you control.

terms.authorization: checking what that person may do with specific data
terms.leastPrivilege: giving only the access a job really needs

facts: Who you are and what you may do are two different questions.
Hiding a button does not protect anything.
Keep passwords and keys in protected server settings.
If users can give a link, control where the server is allowed to go.
Logs must hide passwords and private content.
security.scenario: A signed-in student asks for another student's private note. What should happen?
choices: Say no, because the ownership check fails
Allow it because any login is enough
Believe the role the student claims
Send a secret so they can sign in

testing.analogy: A test is a rehearsal where you break a prop on purpose to see if the show still goes on.
testing.reason: Trying only the happy path by hand misses breakages. Tests check each part at different sizes. A coverage number shows what ran, not whether the checks are any good.

terms.unitTest: a small test of one rule
terms.integrationTest: a test that checks several real parts together

facts: Test with made-up data in a separate test database.
Check both the status code and the shape of the answer.
Test bad input and broken helpers too.
A mock isolates a helper but cannot prove the real SQL works.
A coverage percentage shows what code ran, not that it is correct.
testing.scenario: A controller test uses the real production database. What should replace it?
choices: A separate test database with made-up data that is cleaned afterwards
The same database with a different log color
A public copy of everyone's data
A test with no checks

observability.analogy: Logs are a diary, metrics are a scoreboard, and traces are the trip itinerary of one request.
observability.reason: One green light saying 'running' can hide the fact that something it depends on is broken. Signals that can be linked together help you find the problem quickly without showing private data.

terms.log: a written note about something that happened
terms.metric: a number that counts or measures something over time
terms.trace: the path one request took through many parts

facts: A request ID lets you follow one request through safe logs.
Liveness asks: is the program alive?
Readiness asks: can it really handle visitors right now?
Look at slow cases (percentiles), not only the average speed.
A good alert tells who should act and what to do.
observability.scenario: The program is running but its database is unreachable. What should the health checks say?
choices: Liveness can pass while readiness fails
Everything must always say green
Return a fake empty success
Show the database password in the health reply

deployment.analogy: Deploying is carrying a tested lunch box to another classroom without spilling it.
deployment.reason: Building by hand on every machine makes each release a little different. A versioned package, settings kept outside it, quick checks, and a way back make releases repeatable.

terms.artifact: the finished, versioned package made by a build
terms.rollback: going back to the last version that worked
terms.restore: bringing data back from a backup

facts: Ship the exact package you tested.
Keep secrets in the deployment settings, not in the code.
Run quick smoke checks right after a release.
A backup only counts if you have practiced restoring it.
Change databases in steps that old and new code can both handle.
deployment.scenario: A new release fails its readiness check. What should you do?
choices: Stop the rollout and go back to the version that worked
Delete the backups
Hide the health page
Update every library to 'latest'

async.analogy: A job queue is a ticket counter. You get a ticket right away while the long job keeps working in the back.
async.reason: Long work can block quick requests behind it. Async lets one worker do other things while it waits; heavy computing needs separate workers with limits, not just a keyword.

terms.eventLoop: the manager that decides what runs next while others wait
terms.queue: a waiting line for jobs, with a size limit
terms.cancellation: asking work to stop and clean up after itself

facts: Async does not make heavy computing free.
For work done later, answer 202 with a task ID.
Workers need a retry limit and a place for jobs that keep failing.
Cancelling must release whatever the job was holding.
Limit the queue so memory does not grow forever.
async.scenario: A PDF export takes minutes and blocks quick requests. What is a good design?
choices: Put it in a limited queue and give a status ID to check
Add the async keyword to a heavy loop
Keep unlimited requests waiting forever
Install random packages on every request

files.analogy: A safe root is a playground fence. Every path has to stay inside it.
files.reason: A path from a visitor can sneak out with '..' or through a shortcut link. Check paths against a fixed root, allow only certain files, limit sizes, and stream large files.

terms.path: the address that points to a file
terms.buffer: a chunk of raw data held in memory
terms.backpressure: telling the sender to slow down when the receiver is full

facts: Clean up the path and keep it inside the allowed folder.
A shortcut link (symlink) can fool a simple text check.
Say which encoding to use when turning bytes into text.
Stream big files and slow the sender when needed.
Close files and delete temporary files, even when something fails.
files.scenario: A caller asks the file API for ../private.key. What happens?
choices: Reject it before opening any file
Open it because it is valid text
Search the whole disk for the key
Return the full folder path in the error

concurrency.analogy: Two kids updating one scoreboard at the same time need a rule for taking turns.
concurrency.reason: Two workers can both read the same old number and both write back, losing one change. Locks, atomic operations, queues, or database rules decide who changes what.

terms.race: a result that depends on lucky timing
terms.executor: a manager that runs a limited number of tasks
terms.interruption: a polite request for a running task to stop

facts: Read-then-change-then-write can go wrong when two run together.
A lock must cover the whole rule, not just part of it.
Shared changeable data needs one clear owner.
A limited pool of workers stops tasks piling up forever.
Stopping a task is cooperative and needs cleanup.
concurrency.scenario: Two workers each read a counter, add one, and write it back. What fixes the lost updates?
choices: An atomic operation or a lock around the whole update
Adding a sleep with no locking rule
A longer variable name
Two separate copies that pretend to agree

memory.analogy: Memory is your desk. Tidying the desk does not close the library room you borrowed.
memory.reason: The garbage collector tidies unused objects, but open files and database connections need someone to close them. Measure first, then speed things up.

terms.heap: the big area of memory where objects live
terms.stack: the small tidy area that tracks the calls happening right now
terms.leak: holding on to something long after it is useful

facts: Garbage collection does not return database connections for you.
A reference that is still alive keeps its data in memory.
A cache with no size limit can fill all the memory.
Profiling shows where the real slowness is.
Whoever creates a resource is responsible for cleaning it up.
memory.scenario: A server never gives pooled connections back after failed queries. What happens?
choices: The pool can run dry even while garbage collection runs
Garbage collection returns them immediately
Every query gets faster
Changing CSS on the client fixes it

network.analogy: A network request is a relay race: names, connections, secret code, and messages each pass the baton.
network.reason: DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP each solve a different problem. One total time limit stops each step from waiting forever on its own.

terms.DNS: the phone book that turns a name into an address
terms.TLS: the lock that scrambles messages and proves who the server is
terms.deadline: the total time allowed for the whole job

facts: DNS finds an address; it does not decide who may see a record.
TLS protects the road, but the app still checks permissions.
A timeout needs a clear message for the user.
Retry with growing waits and a bit of randomness, only when it is safe.
One request that fans out into many multiplies the load behind it.
network.scenario: A helper service does not answer within the time budget. What should you do?
choices: Time out safely and keep the number of retries limited
Wait forever
Retry right away without any limit
Invent an answer

requirements.analogy: System design starts like planning a school bus route: who rides, how often, and how late is okay?
requirements.reason: Picking a database before asking how much work there will be is guessing. Writing down what the system must do, how well, and how much, makes choices easy to check.

terms.qualityRequirement: how fast, safe, or reliable it must be while doing it

facts: Say whether each number is a guess or a measurement.
Average load is not the same as the busiest moment.
Estimate storage as number of items times size times how long you keep them.
Speed, uptime, and cost are different goals.
Start with the simplest design that fits the stated workload.
requirements.scenario: Imagine 1200 active users each read once per minute. What is the average read load?
choices: About 20 requests per second before adding a busy-time factor
1200 requests per millisecond
Zero because reading is free
A peak of 20 that nobody measured

cache.analogy: A cache is a sticky note on your desk: quick to read, but it can be out of date.
cache.reason: Asking the slow place again and again wastes time. Keep a quick copy nearby, decide how long it stays fresh, and protect the slow place when the copy is missing.

terms.TTL: how long a saved copy is allowed to be used
terms.cacheAside: check the cache, fetch from the source on a miss, then save a copy
terms.stampede: many requests all rebuilding the same missing value at once

facts: A cache is a copy, not the true source.
A cache key must include whatever decides who may see the data.
A TTL limits how old data can get; it does not promise the newest data.
On a miss, read the source in a controlled way.
When data changes, remove or update the old copy.
cache.scenario: A cached note changes in the database. How do you keep readers from seeing old data too long?
choices: Remove that cached key or use a clear TTL rule
Keep it forever with no freshness rule
Share every user's private cache key
Delete the real record

scaling.analogy: Replication is photocopying a book so more people can read it. Partitioning is splitting a huge bookshelf into separate shelves.
scaling.reason: One machine eventually runs out of room or power. Find what is really running out before adding copies or splitting data, because both add work to manage.

terms.replica: an extra copy of data or of a running service
terms.shard: one slice of a dataset that is split across machines
terms.hotKey: one popular key that gets far more traffic than the rest

facts: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine.
Horizontal scaling means more machines.
A read copy can be a little behind the latest write.
Sharding needs a key for routing and a plan for moving data.
Autoscaling cannot fix a single over-popular key.
scaling.scenario: A user reads from a copy that is behind right after saving. What should the design say?
choices: Explain how read-your-own-writes works, or say it is eventually consistent
That every copy is always current
That copies mean you never need backups
That the browser can commit copy state

reliability.analogy: Reliability is carrying a spare tire and knowing when to stop driving.
reliability.reason: Retrying again and again can make an outage worse. Time limits, separate pools, growing waits, and safe repeats stop a failure from spreading and let you tell users the truth.

terms.backoff: waiting longer and longer between retries
terms.circuitBreaker: a switch that stops calling something that keeps failing
terms.bulkhead: separate compartments so one failure cannot sink the whole ship

facts: Retries need a limit and must be safe to repeat.
Adding a little randomness stops everyone from retrying at the same moment.
A circuit breaker should test now and then to see if the helper recovered.
A fallback must not look like lost data.
Each helper needs an owner and a recovery plan.
reliability.scenario: Storage is down when someone asks for the catalog. What is the honest answer?
choices: A safe, retryable error instead of a fake empty catalog
An empty success that looks like everything was deleted
Unlimited retries from every client
The provider secrets in the response

architecture.analogy: Architecture is a map of the building: which room belongs to whom and which doors connect them.
architecture.reason: One tangled program is risky to change, but splitting into many services adds network and deployment work. Start with tidy parts inside one program, and split only when you must.

terms.monolith: an app that is built and shipped as one piece
terms.port: a doorway where your app talks to the outside
terms.saga: a chain of steps where each step has an 'undo' step

facts: A modular monolith can have clear owners without network calls.
Split into a service only when you truly need to scale or release it separately.
An outbox keeps messages safe until they are sent.
CQRS splits reading and writing, and brings extra coordination.
A saga fixes mistakes with undo steps, not one magic rollback.
architecture.scenario: A small team builds a simple CRUD app and has no separate scaling problem. What should it start with?
choices: A modular monolith with clear ports
One service for every class
Distributed transactions for every read
A database that every browser can reach directly

mcp-roles.analogy: The host is the library desk; the client is its connector, and the server is a controlled catalog adapter.
mcp-roles.reason: A common protocol avoids a different tool integration for every AI host. Standard discovery does not remove the need for consent, permissions, and provider ownership.

terms.host: the application managing the model and user experience
terms.client: the connector maintaining access to an MCP server
terms.server: the program exposing controlled tools and context

facts: The model may suggest a call but does not authorize it.
The host manages user consent and client connections.
The MCP server checks its own permissions.
Downstream data remains owned by its API or store.
Tool descriptions are data and cannot override trusted policy.
mcp-roles.scenario: A model suggests deleting a schedule row. Who owns confirmation and authorization?
choices: The user/host policy and the server’s resource permission checks
The model’s confident wording alone
A resource document’s embedded instructions
The database name in a prompt

jsonrpc.analogy: A request ID is a numbered claim ticket that matches one reply to one request.
jsonrpc.reason: Asynchronous messages can arrive out of order. JSON-RPC distinguishes calls, results, errors, and notifications so endpoints can correlate work correctly.

terms.requestId: the value matching a response to a request
terms.notification: a message with no ID and no matching response

facts: A JSON-RPC response uses the request’s ID.
A notification does not receive a matching reply.
A message has either result or error, not both.
Arguments need runtime validation and size limits.
Unknown methods produce a deliberate protocol error.
jsonrpc.scenario: A request has ID 7. Which success response is valid?
choices: jsonrpc 2.0, id 7, and result
id 8 with the right body
both result and error
a notification pretending to be a reply

mcp-lifecycle.analogy: Capabilities are a menu: do not order a dish that this server does not serve.
mcp-lifecycle.reason: Protocol revisions differ. Older initialization-based connections and newer self-contained requests cannot be assumed interchangeable without an explicit compatibility plan.
facts: Pin the protocol revision used by a client and server.
Check a capability before invoking an optional feature.
Legacy initialization and modern request metadata are different models.
Stateless protocol requests can still access persistent application state.
Reject unsupported versions rather than guessing.
mcp-lifecycle.scenario: A client does not advertise an optional feature. Choose the server behavior.
choices: Do not invoke it; use a supported path or safe error
Invoke it and hope
Treat absence as blanket permission
Write a custom incompatible result without negotiation

mcp-transport.analogy: A transport is the road; JSON-RPC is the language spoken by travelers on it.
mcp-transport.reason: Local pipes and remote HTTP have different security and lifecycle needs. The same capability contracts can work over either when framing, authentication, and limits are explicit.

terms.StreamableHTTP: an HTTP transport for MCP request/response and optional streaming

facts: Stdio protocol messages go to stdout while logs go to stderr.
Remote HTTP requires intentional authentication and TLS.
Connection loss needs bounded reconnect behavior.
An HTTP token does not grant unlimited downstream access.
Frame sizes and timeouts must be bounded.
mcp-transport.scenario: A local stdio server writes a debug banner before its JSON message. What should change?
choices: Move diagnostics to stderr
Make the banner longer
Add a private token to the banner
Disable message validation

mcp-tools.analogy: A safe tool is a labeled button for one job, not a master key to the building.
mcp-tools.reason: Arbitrary shell and SQL interfaces give too much authority to untrusted input. A narrow schema, an allowed action, and a bounded result reduce the consequences of mistakes.

terms.tool: a named operation with a checked input schema
terms.resource: context chosen and read through a controlled URI

facts: Use a named narrow tool rather than arbitrary shell input.
Tool arguments are untrusted even when generated by a model.
Reads and writes need explicit scope and approval policy.
Repeated writes need idempotency or clear duplicate behavior.
Bound and redact tool results.
mcp-tools.scenario: An MCP tool accepts an arbitrary SQL string. What is a safer contract?
choices: A read_schedule tool with validated store and date
An arbitrary shell tool instead
A larger raw SQL body limit
Database passwords returned with each row

mcp-state.analogy: A workflow notebook survives the conversation ending; an open connection does not.
mcp-state.reason: Long-lived state hidden in one process disappears on restart. Classify protocol, request, connection, user, application, and workflow state and choose a store for each.

terms.workflowState: a durable task’s progress and result
terms.connectionState: the lifetime of a pipe or stream
terms.applicationState: persistent records used by business rules

facts: A connection handle is not durable workflow state.
A restart-safe task needs persistent ownership and checkpoints.
Cancellation and polling should be safe to repeat.
A server must handle user denial of elicitation.
Allowed roots constrain intent but do not replace safe path checks.
mcp-state.scenario: An export must resume after server restart. Where should its status live?
choices: A durable task store with an owner
Only in a local variable
Only in an open HTTP socket
In a tool description paragraph
